parts.label: a
parts.technique: Systematic sampling - reason for use
parts.reason: S1.1 explicitly lists systematic sampling among techniques students must know and be able to critique/select, including advantages/disadvantages.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Systematic sampling - interval calculation
parts.reason: S1.1 covers systematic sampling method mechanics.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Systematic sampling - probability of inclusion
parts.reason: Direct consequence of systematic sampling mechanics covered under S1.1.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient calculation
parts.reason: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is not mentioned anywhere in the statements; only Pearson's PMCC is referenced (S5.1) and that explicitly excludes formula-based calculation. Spearman's is a distinct, unmentioned technique.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Hypothesis test on Spearman's rank correlation using critical values
parts.reason: S5.1 only covers hypothesis testing using the product moment correlation coefficient ρ; Spearman's rank correlation test is a different, unmentioned technique with its own critical value tables not referenced in the statements.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Chi-squared goodness-of-fit/association - expected frequency calculation
parts.reason: Contingency table expected frequency calculation for a chi-squared test of association is not mentioned in any statement; S5 only covers binomial proportion and normal mean tests.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Chi-squared test for association
parts.reason: Chi-squared tests (test statistic, degrees of freedom, critical value from chi-squared tables) are not covered by any statement; S5.1-S5.3 list only correlation-coefficient, binomial-proportion, and normal-mean tests.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Unbiased estimates of mean and variance from summary statistics
parts.reason: S2.3 covers calculation of standard deviation/variance from summary statistics (S_xx formula), and unbiased estimate of mean is simply the sample mean; this depth is covered.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Two-sample z-test for difference of means
parts.reason: S5.3 only covers a hypothesis test for the mean of a single Normal distribution with known/assumed variance; a two-sample test for the difference between two population means is not mentioned by any statement.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Stating assumption for two-sample test (equal variance = sample variance)
parts.reason: This part only makes sense in the context of the out-of-spec two-sample test in part (b); also the underlying technique itself is not covered by any statement.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Estimating binomial proportion from frequency data
parts.reason: S4.1 covers using the binomial distribution as a model, and finding the proportion of successes is basic descriptive calculation with the model in mind; this is within the depth of using binomial distribution as a model.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Finding expected frequency r from a goodness-of-fit table
parts.reason: This is the expected-frequency computation used within a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test for a binomial model, a technique not mentioned by any statement.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Chi-squared goodness-of-fit test for binomial model
parts.reason: Chi-squared goodness-of-fit testing (test statistic, degrees of freedom, critical value) is not covered anywhere in the statements; S4.3 only discusses selecting an appropriate distribution qualitatively, not a formal chi-squared test.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Definition/explanation of a statistic
parts.reason: Formal estimation theory (statistics, unbiasedness, bias) is not mentioned in any statement; the whole topic of estimators is absent from the specification list given.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Showing an estimator is biased
parts.reason: Estimator theory (bias, E(R)) is not covered by any statement in the list.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Finding the bias of an estimator
parts.reason: Depends on the out-of-spec result from (b) and the underlying topic (bias of estimators) is not in the statement list.

parts.label: d
parts.technique: Finding constants for unbiased estimators
parts.reason: Unbiased estimator theory is not mentioned anywhere in the statements provided.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Sampling distribution of the mean for a Normal population, standardisation
parts.reason: S5.3 explicitly states the result 'If X~N(μ,σ²) then X̄~N(μ,σ²/n)' as a known fact to be used (no proof required), and this question uses exactly that stated result together with standardisation (P3-level algebra) to form simultaneous equations; the CLT exclusion in S5.3 concerns large-sample approximations for non-Normal populations, not this exact Normal-population result, so the technique is covered.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Finding μ using the sampling distribution result
parts.reason: Directly continues from the in-spec result of (a), using the same stated S5.3 fact about the distribution of the sample mean.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Probability calculation using sampling distribution of the mean
parts.reason: Uses the S5.3 stated distribution of the sample mean together with standardisation to find a probability, consistent with the depth described in that statement.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: Distribution of sum of independent Normal variables
parts.reason: No statement covers linear combinations/sums of independent Normal random variables; S4.2 only covers a single Normal distribution as a model, not addition of independent Normal variables.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: Distribution of difference of independent Normal variables
parts.reason: Combining/differencing independent Normal random variables is not mentioned by any statement; only the single Normal distribution model (S4.2) is covered.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: Linear combination of multiple independent Normal variables
parts.reason: This requires forming and using the distribution of a linear combination of several independent Normal variables, a technique not present in any statement (S4.2 covers only a single Normal distribution model).
